stem:
Urvashi asks whether $\dfrac{9}{25}$ can be written as a terminating decimal by finding an equivalent fraction with denominator $10$, $100$, $1000$, and so on.

One or more options may be correct. Which two claims are correct?

options.text: Multiply numerator and denominator by $4$ to get the equivalent fraction $\dfrac{36}{100}$.
$\dfrac{9}{25}$ can be written as the terminating decimal $0.36$.
$\dfrac{9}{25}$ cannot become a terminating decimal because $25$ is not already $10$, $100$, or $1000$.
Writing $0.36$ is what creates the original fraction $\dfrac{9}{25}$.

teacher.key_rationale: An equivalent fraction with denominator $100$ is $\dfrac{36}{100}$, so $\dfrac{9}{25}=0.36$. The denominator need not start as $10$, $100$, or $1000$; the decimal form does not create the original fraction.
